extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in a real analysis / metric spaces course (e.g., Math 104)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of textbook-style exercises and proof prompts in real analysis covering metric spaces, sequences, limits, series, and power series; intended as homework/problems to prove statements, construct counterexamples, and follow hints provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness implies closedness (3.3 (a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if X is a metric space and Y ⊆ X is complete (as a metric space in the induced metric), then Y is closed in X. Also show that Theorem 2.34 and the result of 2.3:6 follow from this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof: show every limit point of Y (in X) is in Y by taking a convergent Cauchy sequence in Y and using completeness to get its limit in Y. The exercise invites deriving earlier results from this fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subset of a complete space is complete (3.3 (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if X is complete and Y is closed in X, then Y (with the subspace metric) is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a Cauchy sequence in Y, view it in X, use completeness of X to get limit in X, and closedness of Y to conclude the limit lies in Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of completeness by closedness in embeddings (3.3 (c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Show: if Y is a metric space such that for every metric space X containing Y, Y is closed in X, then Y is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approach: prove the contrapositive—if Y is not complete, adjoin a point q to Y to form X ∪ {q} and define a metric making q a limit point of Y but q ∉ Y. Remarks mention Rudin constructions (completion) as alternate routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete bounded (connected) need not be compact (3.3:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show the metric space described in 2:R10 is bounded and complete, but not compact. (b) Find a connected metric space that is bounded and complete but not compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive/counterexample tasks: exhibit explicit metric spaces. For (a) refer to exercise 2:R10; for (b) think of non-compact complete connected bounded examples (e.g., infinite-dimensional or specially designed metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential test for Cauchy sequences (3.3:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Give an example showing that the condition lim_{n→∞} d(s_n, s_{n+1}) = 0 is not equivalent to (sn) being Cauchy; show one implication may hold but the other can fail. (b) Investigate whether there exists a sequence of index-pairs ((m_k,n_k)) such that for every sequence (s_n) the condition lim_{k→∞} d(s_{m_k}, s_{n_k}) = 0 is equivalent to (s_n) being Cauchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a): produce concrete counterexamples. Part (b): try various sequences of index pairs; analyze pitfalls where sequences can satisfy one condition without being Cauchy or vice versa. The suggestion: identify properties of the index pairs that lead to either difficulty and use them to build or rule out such sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse to sequential compactness implies compactness (3.3:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove: if every sequence in metric space X has a convergent subsequence, then X is compact. Provide the proof without machinery used earlier in the text, following indicated steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps given: define f(x) = sup{ε ≤ 1: some G_α contains N_ε(x)} and show f is continuous and positive-valued. Show inf_x f(x) > 0 (contradiction if 0 via sequence with f(x_n)→0). Choose c < inf f(x) and show one can select a finite subcover; if not, produce sequence with pairwise distances ≥ c which cannot have a convergent subsequence. Use these to conclude X is compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper and lower limits — basic exercises (3.4:0, 3:R4, 3:R5 references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises about lim sup and lim inf of sequences: determining upper/lower limits, and properties of lim sup of sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes an added part (b) asking for an example where inequalities can be strict. Refer to Rudin's related problems; typical tasks: compute lim sup/lim inf, provide examples showing strict inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequence behaviour for lim sup/lim inf (3.4:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show that if a sequence (s_n) converges to s, then every subsequence converges to s. (b) Show inequalities relating lim sup/lim inf of a subsequence to those of the full sequence and give examples where inequalities are strict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalize: lim sup_{k→∞} s_{n_k} ≤ lim sup_{n→∞} s_n and lim inf_{k→∞} s_{n_k} ≥ lim inf_{n→∞} s_n; produce strict examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting lim sup as limit of suprema (3.4:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show lim sup a_n = lim_{m→∞} (sup_{n≥m} a_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful with extended real values: either assume suprema are finite or state behavior when some suprema are ±∞. Standard proof using monotone sequences of suprema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic of possibly infinite limits (3.4:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend basic limit arithmetic to extended real limits: if x_n→a and y_n→b (where a,b may be ±∞), show that if a+b (or a·b) is defined then x_n+y_n→a+b (or x_n y_n→a b). Various parts (a)-(f) treat cases, sketch proofs, and construct counterexamples when operations are undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove core finite cases, then reduce other finite/infinite cases using sign changes and known results; sketch harder parts and construct sequence examples showing non-existence of limits when sums/products are undefined. Use Rudin's earlier theorems where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every real sequence has a subsequence approaching an extended real (3.4:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show every real sequence has either a convergent subsequence, a subsequence tending to +∞, or a subsequence tending to –∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard diagonalization or Bolzano–Weierstrass type arguments applied to bounded/unbounded cases; relate to lim sup/lim inf results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite cube as k-dimensional extended real line analog (3.4:5)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show every sequence in R^k has a subsequence converging in (R ∪ {−∞,+∞})^k (componentwise). (b) Define addition and dot-product operations where possible so limits are respected and determine when such operations can be defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use componentwise application of 3.4:4; analyze which componentwise combinations admit well-defined algebraic operations respecting sequence limits and give counterexamples otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite ball as another k-dimensional 'infinite point' model (3.4:6)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Define notion x_n → a_∞ meaning |x_n|→∞ and x_n/|x_n|→a (|a|=1). (a)-(e) ask to show subsequence existence, define operations involving infinite points where possible, and show obstructions for mixing different directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show any unbounded sequence has a subsequence with a direction on the unit sphere; analyze addition and dot-product definitions for infinite points and give counterexamples where definitions cannot respect limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of the two k-dimensional 'infinite' notions (3.4:7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give examples showing a sequence can approach a point in the (R∪{±∞})^k sense but not approach any a_∞ in the infinite-ball sense, and vice versa. Characterize which points have mutual implications and show every unbounded sequence has subsequences approaching both kinds of points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit sequences exhibiting the phenomena; characterize points p in (R∪{±∞})^k and directions a on the unit sphere a for which the implication holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomparable sets of natural numbers (3.4:8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in(S,n) and out(S,n) counts; (a) if S⊂T show inequality of lim sup(in−out) unless both ±∞; (b) construct family A of subsets S with lim sup(in−out)=0 and show maximal/inclusion properties and that any S either contains a member of A or is contained in a member of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial/limsup reasoning; show no member of A is proper subset of another and prove the dichotomy via constructive or combinatorial arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special sequences true/false and examples (3.5:0, 3.5:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (3.5:0) True/false problems about special sequences. (3.5:1) Show limits such as lim n^{1/n} = 1, lim n^{1000} (1.001)^{-n} = +∞, and discuss lim n^{n−p} behavior for positive p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard tools (logs, comparisons, known limits). For some statements, Rudin proves specific cases; refer to those for p=1 and extend or disprove for general p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series convergence basics and true/false (3.6:0, references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various true/false questions and convergence tests for series; reference Rudin exercises R6, R14, R15, R19. (3.6:0) includes statements about boundedness of partial sums implying convergence, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by constructing series or applying known convergence criteria; use partial sums, comparison tests, and known counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization of Theorem 3.24 to R^2 regions (3.6:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the theorem on nonnegative-term series (Theorem 3.24) generalizes to series in R^2 when 'nonnegative' is replaced by each of three candidate cones E1, E2, E3 defined geometrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each set E1={(x,y):x≥0,y≥0}, E2={(x,y):x≥0,x+y≥0}, E3={(x,y):x+|y|≥0}, determine truth by drawing pictures and proving or giving counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicative infinite products and relation to sum of (a_n−1) (3.6:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show that if either all a_n>1 or all a_n<1 (positive), then product ∏ a_n converges iff ∑(a_n−1) converges. (b) Give counterexamples when signs vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) reduces to log transformations or comparison; for (b) suggest sequences 1+c_n,1−c_n alternating to make sum and product behaviors differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor set and 2-adic metric mapping (3.6:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a map f from nonnegative integers (binary digits reversed, 1→2) to the Cantor set; show it is an isometry between (Z,2-adic metric) and (Cantor set,d) and that f(N) is dense in the Cantor set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out the digit manipulations and compute distances; use properties of ternary/binary expansions to show equality of distances and density.

rubrics_metrics.name: The space l^2 of square-summable sequences (3.6:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define l^2, show scalar multiples and sums stay in l^2, define inner product and metric, show e_n sequences have components converging to 0 yet do not converge in l^2, and show l^2 is complete (a Hilbert space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cauchy/Schwarz and Theorem 1.37 for estimates. For completeness show every Cauchy sequence in l^2 has coordinatewise limits whose squares sum converges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence result for series to ±∞ (3.6:5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (a_n) and (b_n) satisfy a_n ≤ b_n and ∑ a_n does not converge and is not −∞, then show ∑ b_n does not converge; explore conventions Σ a_n = ±∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison of partial sums and monotonicity; consider cases where partial sums are unbounded above to force divergence of the larger series.

rubrics_metrics.name: No boundary between convergent and divergent positive-term series (3.7:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) From Rudin's facts show no 'boundary sequence' exists. (b)-(c) Provide simpler constructions (given a divergent/convergent series, construct a faster-decaying divergent sequence or slower-decaying convergent sequence) using sequences of partial sums An, Bn with specified differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sequences B_n from A_n or vice versa with square-root scaling and manipulate differences to show existence of sequences decaying faster/slower while preserving divergence/convergence; explicit constructive proofs replace Rudin's more complicated constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot test Σ a_n for convergence just from values at special indices (3.7:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Construct two decreasing positive sequences a_n and b_n with same values at n=2^k such that Σ a_n converges but Σ b_n diverges. (b) Identify the fallacy in replacing the full series by sampled blocks in an argument using sampling at powers of 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build sequences by prescribing values on dyadic indices then interpolate to get extremes; show the 'sampling' equivalence fails without extra regularity hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizing sampling convergence test; sufficient condition (3.7:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a decreasing nonnegative sequence a_n and strictly increasing integers n_k, prove inequalities relating sums over blocks and deduce that if ratios (n_{k+1}−n_k)/(n_k−n_{k−1}) are bounded then convergence of Σ a_n is equivalent to convergence of Σ (n_{k+1}−n_k) a_{n_k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove block-sum inequalities (part (a)), deduce implications, and conclude bounded-ratio criterion yields equivalence; use earlier counterexample as illustration when ratios unbounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and sufficient sampling condition via subsequences (3.7:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Exhibit example where previous sufficient condition fails to be necessary. (b) Prove a condition (existence of subsequence with bounded block-ratio set) that is necessary and sufficient for sampling-test equivalence across all decreasing positive sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct special index sequence {n_k} combining powers of 2 to show subtleties. For (b) follow hint to prove equivalences (i)⇒(ii)⇒(iii)⇒(iv)⇒(i) and use contrapositive ideas for hardest implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series testability by sampling under extra monotonicity (3.7:5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show sampling argument can be made to work if an additional strong monotonicity condition a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ... ≥ a_{2^k} ≥ ... holds, implying equivalence between Σ a_n and Σ sampled series Σ 2^k a_{2^k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monotonicity across dyadic blocks to control sums; deduce convergence equivalences for sequences meeting the stronger hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of distances for a convergent sequence (3.7:6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (p_n) in metric space X converges to p, show (a) d(p_1,p) ≤ Σ d(p_n,p_{n+1}), (b) for any ε>0 there exists subsequence with partial sums close to d(p_1,p), and (c) the converse implication (Σ d(p_n,p_{n+1}) convergent ⇒ (p_n) convergent) is false in general; produce counterexample in a familiar metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triangle inequality for (a). For (c) look for standard counterexamples (e.g., space with 'jumps' or sequences wandering along disjoint points while adjacent distances summable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Root and ratio tests true/false preliminaries (3.9:0)
rubrics_metrics.description: True/false questions exploring limits lim sup |a_{n+1}/a_n| equal to given values and implications for convergence/divergence of Σ a_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate statements via known behavior of ratio/root tests and counterexamples when lim sup is boundary value 1 or when conditions vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharper tests analogous to ratio/root tests (3.9:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For a_n = n^{−p} show −lim (log a_n)/(log n) = p and derive test: for general positive a_n let p = −lim sup (log a_n)/(log n); if p>1 then Σ a_n converges. (d),(e) give complementary statements involving lim n(1−a_{n+1}/a_n) and p = lim n(1−a_{n+1}/a_n). Parts ask what happens when these tests are applied where root/ratio tests already suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tests compare to model n^{−p}; proofs use logs and asymptotics. Some parts are easier if logarithm properties are allowed; part (e) (ratio-style refinement) may require calculus/differentiation to prove fully but can be stated and applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified ratio test with lag c (3.9:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Show Σ a_n converges if for some positive integer c, lim sup |a_{n+c}/a_n| < 1. (b) Show this holds with c=2 for certain example series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization of ratio test: consider subsequences every c steps and apply root/ratio-type estimates to products across blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series convergence location questions (3.10:0)
rubrics_metrics.description: True/false style: if ∑ c_n z^n converges at z=1+3i, must it also converge at z=2+2i? (relates to radius/region of convergence geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use notion of radius of convergence (disk centered at 0); check whether |2+2i| ≤ |1+3i| etc.; compare magnitudes to determine inclusion in disc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series and ratio test relations (3.10:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If |c_n/c_{n+1}| tends to a limit (finite or +∞) then that limit equals radius of convergence. (b)-(c) Obtain inequalities relating lim sup and lim inf of |c_n/c_{n+1}| to the radius when limits don't exist. (d) Analyze a specific constructed coefficient sequence c_{2^k}=c_{2^k+1}=2^k to verify inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard root/ratio formulas for radius of convergence and handle lim sup/lim inf subtleties; part (d) is a concrete verification using theorem 3.39.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summation by parts true/false examples (3.11:0)
rubrics_metrics.description: True/false style questions about alternating and grouped series, e.g., convergence of series with periodic numerators and use of summation by parts consequences (relying on Rudin's R7 and R8 references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply summation by parts (Abel transformation) and Schwarz/Cauchy inequalities where needed; construct counterexamples to false statements.
